An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name is merged into it variant by variant: an own variant carrying a shipped variant's name replaces that variant in place, and every other own variant joins after the shipped ones. The shipped variants the own recipe does not name stay as they are, and the own recipe always writes its variants in the shipped file's variant form, each named. It gives both moves with no extra syntax, overriding one shipped variant or adding one, while every variant the person did not touch keeps following the shipped file, which matches the variant-grained edits the settings view makes. The name now has to be matched at two levels, recipe and variant, so a mistyped variant name silently adds a variant instead of replacing one, a person cannot remove a shipped variant without some further rule, and the own file has to spell variant names in whatever form the sibling question on the shipped variant format settles.

An own recipe carrying a shipped recipe's name declares what it does, through one line between its heading and its block like the existing `Stage:` line: one value makes it replace every variant of the shipped recipe, the other makes its variants join the shipped ones, and a recipe declaring nothing takes one fixed default of the two. Each person chooses per recipe between taking a recipe over and adding to it, so neither the copying cost of whole replacement nor the inability to remove shipped variants under joining is forced on everyone. It adds a second declaration line the reader must parse, the README must document, and a person must know about, and which of the two behaviours the undeclared default takes still has to be chosen, an existing own recipe falling under it unchanged.

An own recipe no longer touches a shipped recipe of its name: the shipped recipe keeps all its variants, and the own recipe of the colliding name is drawn as a non-runnable entry naming the collision and its file, as a recipe with an unknown placeholder is drawn today, so a hand-written recipe must take a name of its own. Changing a shipped recipe's variants is left to the settings view alone. A name then means exactly one recipe, so the pane's start-by-name check, the fixed-name buttons, and the merge need no rule for a collision, and the settings view becomes the one place a shipped recipe's variants are changed. It removes a capability the extension ships today, replacing a recipe by hand, the seven fixed-name button recipes included, and turns every existing own recipe of a shipped name into a dead entry; it is viable only as far as the settings view's own edits reach shipped variants, which the sibling question on editing shipped variants settles.

open-question.question: The mission page groups its recipe buttons today under the headings Claude Code, Antigravity, and Your recipes, the last holding a person's own recipes that replace no shipped one. A page then holds one unheaded run of buttons followed by one headed group, which reads unevenly, and on a page whose step holds few or no own recipes the heading marks a distinction a person may not care about; where edited variants of shipped recipes are kept, and whether an own recipe of a shipped name joins as a variant, are settled by the Variant store file and Own recipe replacement questions, and either can leave the group holding little.

One flat list under the Recipes heading with no group heading and no mark: the shipped recipes in the shipped file's order (own replacements in place), then the own recipes that replace no shipped one appended in the own file's order, every button drawn alike. It is the simplest page once the host groups go: one uniform run of buttons per mission page, short already because the pane narrows each page to the step its diagram fills, and the reader's `own` group value and the page's group table can be removed outright rather than kept for one heading. One flat list under the Recipes heading with no group heading: the shipped recipes in the shipped file's order (own replacements in place, unmarked as today), then the own recipes that replace no shipped one appended in the own file's order, each of those buttons carrying a small mark (a tag or a distinct style) saying it comes from the person's own recipe file. It gets the flat list's even layout while keeping what the separate group gave, telling at a glance which buttons are the person's own, without spending a heading on a group that may hold one button or none on a given page. It adds a per-button mark the page does not draw today, one more element beside the label the Button label content question fills with harness, model, and effort and beside the variant dropdown, so the button grows busier, and it still reverses the first version's recorded decision of a group of its own.

One flat list under the Recipes heading with no group heading, every recipe, shipped and own alike, sorted by name so own recipes stand interleaved among the shipped ones, each own recipe that replaces no shipped one carrying a mark saying it comes from the person's own file. A person finds a recipe by its name in one predictable order whatever file it came from, and an own recipe written for the same purpose as a shipped one lands beside it rather than at the end of the list. It discards the shipped file's own order, which places related recipes in a deliberate sequence (the normal execution recipe before the critical one, a chain's steps in workflow order), so the page's order changes with every name, and it needs a sort the reader and the page do not have today, on top of the mark and the reversal of the first version's own-group decision.

open-question.question: The variant a person selects in a recipe's dropdown is to be remembered, and the extension today stores nothing beyond the page's `setState`, which lasts only while the panel stays open. Per what is the selection remembered (the recipe everywhere, the recipe in one project, or the recipe on one mission), and where is it kept so that it outlasts the pane?
open-question.alternative: The selection is remembered per recipe name across every project. It is kept in the extension's `ExtensionContext.globalState` as a map from recipe name to variant name, written by the extension each time the page posts a new dropdown choice and read when the pane posts a mission's recipes. A remembered variant that no longer exists falls back to the recipe's default. No file is written for it. One selection follows the person into every project and mission and survives a window reload or a restart. VS Code's own storage holds it, so no file needs a format, a writer, or protection against hand edits, and it stays separate from the variants and settings a person edits on purpose. A choice made for one project's work changes what every other project's button runs, so a critical execution variant picked in one place silently carries over to routine work elsewhere. It is also the extension's first use of stored state, which the person can neither see nor edit outside the dropdown.

alternative.id: Per recipe user-wide in the variant file

open-question.alternative: The selection is remembered per recipe name across every project. It is kept as an entry in the per-user file the settings view writes its variants to, rewritten there each time the dropdown changes and read with the recipes on every re-read of the pane. Every per-user choice about variants stands in one readable file the person can inspect, copy to another machine, or fix by hand, and the remembered selection is read with the variants it names, so a stale name is visible beside them. Every dropdown click rewrites a file that also holds hand-editable variant lines, so a click races a hand edit and churns the file. It depends on which file holds the variants and in what format, which the variant-store question owns, and it holds the remembered selection close to each recipe's default, whose precedence the default-versus-remembered question owns.

alternative.id: Per recipe user-wide in user settings

open-question.alternative: The selection is remembered per recipe name across every project. It is kept in a new setting the manifest contributes at application scope, an object from recipe name to variant name, written with the configuration API at the global target each time the dropdown changes. The selection is visible and editable in the person's `settings.json` beside `gurita.ownRecipesFile`, and VS Code's Settings Sync carries it to the person's other machines with no work of the extension's own. Every dropdown click writes the person's user settings file, which is meant for configuration rather than UI state, and each write raises a settings-change event that other extensions and an open settings editor see. Like every user-wide scope, one project's choice changes every other project's.

alternative.id: Per recipe per project in workspaceState

open-question.alternative: The selection is remembered per recipe name within one project, the workspace the pane was opened on, and shared by every mission of that project. It is kept in the extension's `ExtensionContext.workspaceState` as a map from recipe name to variant name. Nothing is written into the project's tree. Each project keeps its own working habit (one project run on its critical execution variant, another on its routine one) across reloads and restarts, while every mission in the project, a newly defined one included, opens on the variant last chosen there. The repository stays clean. Two live missions of one project that need different variants, for example one in a critical scope and one routine, share one selection and overwrite each other's choice. A new project starts at every recipe's default again, and the stored state is invisible outside the dropdown.

alternative.id: Per recipe per mission in workspaceState

open-question.alternative: The selection is remembered per recipe name on one mission, keyed by the mission's path as the pane lists it, within the project's `ExtensionContext.workspaceState`, as a map from mission path and recipe name to variant name. Nothing is written into the project's tree. The scope matches the page: each mission's page shows its own selection, so missions of different weight in one project keep different variants without overwriting each other, and switching mission tabs never changes what another mission's button runs. Every newly defined mission opens on the defaults again, so a person who always uses one variant reselects it on every mission. Entries for finished missions are never cleared, and a later mission defined at the same path, which the definition tool allows once the earlier directory is gone, inherits the finished mission's selections.

alternative.id: Per mission falling back to the project

open-question.alternative: The selection is remembered on two levels in `ExtensionContext.workspaceState`: per recipe on each mission, keyed by the mission's path, and per recipe for the project as the variant last selected on any of its missions. A mission's own selection wins; a mission with none for a recipe opens on the project's last selection, and only a project with none opens on the default. Missions keep their own selections when they differ, while a new mission inherits the variant the person has been using in the project instead of reverting to the default. Which variant a button opens on depends on a two-level rule the page does not show, so a selection made on one mission silently changes what an untouched new mission starts with. It carries the per-mission option's stale entries for finished paths, and its fallback overlaps the precedence of the default, which the default-versus-remembered question owns.

alternative.id: Kept in the page state only

open-question.alternative: The selection is not stored outside the page. It is remembered per recipe on each mission inside the webview's `setState`, beside the selected mission and each question view's position, so it lasts while the panel exists and is lost when the panel is closed or the window reloads. The settings view's default variant is then the only choice that outlasts the pane. Nothing new is stored and no storage mechanism is introduced. The lasting choice has one home, the default the settings view picks, and the dropdown is a per-session override that cannot leave a forgotten selection running on later work. It rejects the premise that the selection outlasts the pane: closing the panel or reloading the window resets every button to its default, so a person who works on one variant reselects it every session. That leaves the goal's remembered choice met only as far as the page state reaches.

open-question.question: The settings view picks each recipe's default variant, and the mission page remembers the variant last selected in the recipe's dropdown. When does the default decide which variant a button runs: only until a first selection is remembered, or does picking a new default also replace a remembered selection?
open-question.alternative: The default the settings view picks decides a recipe button's variant only while no dropdown selection is remembered for it. A remembered selection always wins over the default, and picking a new default in the settings view leaves every remembered selection as it stands. A remembered variant that no longer exists (deleted or renamed in the settings view) is dropped and the button falls back to the current default. A person's own dropdown choice is never overridden by something done elsewhere: the button runs what that person last chose, and the rule is one plain precedence, with the default needing no write to the remembered store and the remembered store no reaction to a default change. Once a selection is remembered, a new default has no visible effect on that recipe's button, so a person who changes the default in the settings view and expects the button to follow sees nothing change and must reselect in the dropdown itself; how many buttons are affected depends on the reach the sibling question on the remembered choice's scope gives a selection.

Picking a new default for a recipe in the settings view clears every remembered selection of that recipe, so its button runs the new default until a later dropdown selection is remembered again. Between default changes a remembered selection wins over the default, and a remembered variant that no longer exists falls back to the default. The settings view's default pick always takes effect at once on the button, which matches the plain reading of setting a default, while a dropdown choice still lasts for as long as no new default is picked. A deliberate dropdown choice of a non-default variant is silently lost whenever the default changes, even when the person changed the default for a different reason; where the remembered choice is kept per project or per mission (the sibling scope question), one default change clears selections on many pages at once.

A remembered selection is kept only for a variant other than the default: selecting the current default in the dropdown removes the remembered selection, so the button then follows the default and moves with a later default change, while a remembered non-default variant stays across default changes. A remembered variant that no longer exists falls back to the default. Each case behaves as intended: a person who never left the default, or returned to it, tracks the new default, and a person who deliberately chose another variant keeps it, with no choice lost and no new default left without effect for those who were on the old one. The rule is less obvious than either plain precedence: whether a default change moves a button depends on whether the selection happened to be the old default, which the dropdown alone does not show, and if the new default is the variant a person had remembered, that selection becomes indistinguishable from following the default.

There is one stored choice per recipe rather than two: selecting a variant in the button's dropdown sets that recipe's default, and picking the default in the settings view changes the same value, so the last write from either place decides which variant the button runs. A variant that no longer exists falls back to the first variant left. No precedence rule exists to be learned or misread: the dropdown and the settings view always show the same variant, and the button runs exactly what both show. The default and the remembered selection become one value held at one reach, which is viable only if the sibling question on the remembered choice's scope keeps the selection as widely as the default is kept; a selection made on one mission page then changes the button on every page the default reaches, and the settings view's default pick stops being a separate fallback.

open-question.question: The settings view duplicates, renames, and deletes variants and changes each line's model and effort, storing the result in a per-user file. Do those edits apply to a shipped variant directly, the stored copy standing in for the shipped one, or are shipped variants read-only, so that only a duplicate can be renamed, deleted, or changed?
open-question.alternative: Every edit the settings view offers applies to a shipped variant as it does to a duplicate. Changing a line's model or effort or renaming the variant writes a stored copy to the per-user file that stands in for the shipped variant and keeps its place in the recipe's dropdown. Deleting it writes a record there that hides it. The stored copy and the hiding record stay until the person resets the variant, and resetting removes them so the shipped variant shows again. One rule for every variant: a person who wants the shipped `First run` on `sonnet` changes that line where it stands, with no copy to make and no second entry crowding the dropdown, and a variant they never use can be taken out of the dropdown entirely. The stored copy holds the shipped lines as they were on the day of the edit, so a later extension version that changes that variant's lines (a new skill in the chain, a corrected flag) is silently masked until the person resets it. The extension also needs a stable way to match a stored copy or hiding record to the shipped variant it replaces, and that match must still hold after a rename. Whether that identity can be read depends on how the shipped file names its variants and on how own recipes of a shipped name are treated, both owned by sibling questions. Deleting the shipped default, or a recipe's last variant, needs a rule of its own.

Shipped variants cannot be edited: their lines, names, and presence in the dropdown stay exactly as the shipped file gives them. The settings view only offers to duplicate a shipped variant (and to pick it as the default, which changes the recipe, not the variant). Renaming, deleting, and changing a line's model and effort apply only to the duplicates stored in the per-user file. Nothing in the per-user file ever stands in for a shipped line, so every shipped variant always runs what the installed extension ships, updates included. The store holds only the person's own variants, so no identity match, reset action, or hiding record is needed, and the reader adds the stored variants beside the shipped ones without replacing anything. A person who wants a shipped chain on another model has to duplicate it first and then sees both in the dropdown, with no way to drop the shipped original they no longer use. Across 24 shipped recipes, some of them sibling Antigravity copies, the dropdowns grow with every adjustment. A duplicate also freezes the shipped lines it was copied from, so the person's copy still misses later shipped changes.

A shipped variant's lines can have their model and effort changed in place: the stored copy in the per-user file stands in for the shipped variant until the person resets it. Its name cannot be changed and it cannot be deleted. Renaming and deleting apply only to duplicates. It covers the most common adjustment, a different model or effort on a chain the person keeps using, without a duplicate. Because a shipped variant keeps its own name, the stored copy matches the variant it replaces by that name, and a default or remembered selection naming it never points at a variant that was renamed away or deleted. It splits the settings view's actions into two rules, one for shipped variants and one for duplicates, which the view must show per action. A changed shipped variant still masks later shipped changes to its lines until it is reset. A variant the person never uses stays in the dropdown. Matching by name works only if the shipped file gives each variant a name of its own, the format a sibling question settles.

A shipped variant's lines can have their model and effort changed in place through a stored copy that stands in for it, and the variant can be deleted, which stores a record that hides it. Its name cannot be changed. Reset removes the stored copy or the hiding record. Renaming applies only to duplicates. A person can both adjust a shipped chain and remove the shipped variants they never run from their dropdowns, while the variant's name stays a fixed key for the stored copy, the hiding record, the default, and the remembered selection, so no rename has to be followed. Every drawback of a stored copy standing in applies: later shipped line changes are masked until reset, and a reset action is needed. It also needs a rule for hiding the variant that is the recipe's default, one a mission page remembers, or the recipe's last variant. Hiding overlaps with what disabling a harness may do to the variants that hold that harness's lines, the effect a sibling question owns.

A shipped variant's lines and name stay as shipped and cannot be edited. The one change the settings view allows to a shipped variant is deleting it, which stores a record in the per-user file that hides it from the dropdown until the person restores it. Changing lines and renaming apply only to duplicates. Every shipped variant that shows still runs exactly what the installed extension ships, updates included, while the person can still declutter a dropdown, for example by dropping the shipped variant they replaced with a duplicate. A hiding record carries no lines, so it cannot go stale. Adjusting a shipped chain still needs a duplicate, so the duplicate-then-hide pair is two actions where a direct edit would be one. The duplicate freezes the shipped lines it was copied from, and once its original is hidden a later shipped change is out of sight altogether. A hiding record still needs a stable identity for the shipped variant and a rule for hiding the default or the last variant.

open-question.question: A recipe button is to show the harness, models, and efforts of the selected variant, read from its lines. A variant may hold several lines that differ in model and effort (the shipped `First run` runs `fable` at `xhigh` and `opus` at `high`), and one shipped chain mixes `agy` and `claude` lines. What does the button show for such a variant: every line's values in line order, or each distinct harness, model, and effort once?
open-question.alternative: The label lists one entry per line of the variant, in line order, each entry that line's harness, model, and effort, repeats included: the shipped `First run` reads claude fable xhigh, claude fable xhigh, claude opus high, claude fable xhigh, and the mixed-agent chain opens with its `agy` entry ahead of its three `claude` entries. Nothing is merged or counted. The label is a faithful, position-for-position reading of the lines, so a person sees exactly which step of the chain runs on which harness, model, and effort without opening the hover, and the reading needs no merging rule to test or explain. The label grows with the chain and repeats itself: the four-line shipped chains give four near-identical entries, which makes the buttons long and hard to compare at a glance in a list that today shows only a name per button, while the hover already carries the lines as written.

The label keeps line order but merges consecutive lines whose harness, model, and effort are all equal into one entry; a combination that recurs after a different one is listed again. `First run` reads claude fable xhigh, claude opus high, claude fable xhigh; `Prepare tasks` reads claude fable high, claude fable xhigh. It still shows the order in which the chain switches harness, model, or effort, the one thing a set-based label loses, while removing the run of identical entries that makes a per-line label long. A combination that alternates with another is still listed more than once, so the label's length depends on how the chain happens to be ordered rather than on how many distinct settings it uses, and the merging is a rule a reader of the label has to infer.

The label lists each distinct combination of harness, model, and effort once, in the order of its first appearance in the lines, with no count or position: `First run` reads claude fable xhigh, claude opus high, and the mixed-agent chain reads agy gemini-4-argon medium, claude opus high, claude fable xhigh, claude fable high. Every combination that actually runs is shown with its pairing intact, so a person can tell which model runs at which effort on which harness, at a length bounded by the number of distinct settings rather than the number of lines. The label no longer says which step uses which combination or how many steps use each, so a variant whose only change is moving one step to another model may read the same as before, and a chain with many distinct settings still yields a long label.

The label shows the distinct harnesses once, the distinct models once, and the distinct efforts once, each as its own list in the order of first appearance and independent of the others: `First run` reads claude · fable, opus · xhigh, high, and the mixed-agent chain reads agy, claude · gemini-4-argon, opus, fable · medium, high, xhigh. It is the shortest label that still names every value the variant uses, with a fixed three-part shape that is easy to scan and compare across buttons, and on the common single-harness, single-setting variant it collapses to one harness, one model, and one effort. It drops the pairings: a reader cannot tell which model runs at which effort, and on a mixed chain which model belongs to which harness, so two variants with swapped pairings show the same label.

alternative.id: Per harness, its distinct models and efforts

open-question.alternative: The label names each distinct harness once, in order of first appearance, and after each the distinct models and the distinct efforts of that harness's lines: the mixed-agent chain reads agy: gemini-4-argon / medium; claude: opus, fable / high, xhigh, and a single-harness variant reads like the per-field form. It keeps the binding that matters most on a mixed chain, which models run on which harness, at nearly the length of the per-field label, and it reads naturally beside a settings view that holds model and effort lists per harness. Model and effort are still unpaired within a harness, so on `First run` it cannot say that fable runs at xhigh and opus at high, and the grouped form is longer and more nested than a flat label on a button.

The label shows a field's value only when every line shares it and otherwise a short count or mark in its place (for example claude · 2 models · 2 efforts for `First run`, 2 harnesses · 3 models · 3 efforts for the mixed-agent chain), the full per-line values left to the button's hover text, which already carries the lines as written. Every button stays short and of one shape whatever the chain's length, and a single-setting variant still reads its exact harness, model, and effort, so the list stays scannable while nothing is hidden beyond one hover. For exactly the multi-line variants the question is about, the label stops showing the models and efforts the goal asks it to show, and two variants differing only in which models they use read identically until hovered.

open-question.question: The extension is to read each line's harness, model, and effort from the line's own text. A variant may hold a line that carries none of them or not all: a shell step of the person's own, the looped recipe's slot line `<single-task line>`, a command of a harness the extension does not know, or a harness line written without `--model` or `--effort`. How is such a line treated on the recipe button and in the settings view's line editor?
open-question.alternative: On the recipe button, each line adds only the values its text carries: a `claude` or `agy` line without `--model` or `--effort` adds its harness and whichever flag it holds, while a shell step, the slot line `<single-task line>`, and a line of a command the extension does not know add nothing, so a variant none of whose lines is readable, the shipped looped recipe among them, shows its name alone. In the line editor, only a line of a known harness carrying both `--model` and `--effort` gets model and effort controls; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. The extension never invents a value and never writes a flag a line did not already carry, so the only rewrite it makes is replacing a value already in the text, the smallest step away from the draft's rule that it composes no line. The button silently understates what a variant runs: it cannot tell a harness's default model from a line that runs no harness at all, and the looped recipe's button says nothing of what its tasks run on. A harness line written without a flag can never be given a model or effort in the settings view.

On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each gap: `default` for a model or effort a known-harness line leaves out, one fixed mark (such as "other step") for a shell step or a line of a command the extension does not know, and one fixed mark (such as "per task") for the slot line `<single-task line>`. In the line editor, only a line of a known harness carrying both `--model` and `--effort` gets model and effort controls; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. The button tells the person truthfully what each part of a variant runs on, including that a step runs outside any harness or on the harness's own default, while the extension still writes only values already in a line. The marks are a small vocabulary of their own to name, draw, and test, and they lengthen labels whose shape the button-label sibling decides. A flagless harness line stays uneditable, so the person must hand-write the flag in an own recipe to get controls.

On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each gap: `default` for a model or effort a known-harness line leaves out, one fixed mark for a shell step or a line of a command the extension does not know, and one fixed mark (such as "per task") for the slot line. In the line editor, every line of a known harness gets model and effort controls, a missing value shown as the harness default, and setting one inserts the flag into the line's text ahead of its closing `;` and any `# interactive` comment; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. Every line that runs a harness the extension knows can have its model and effort set, so no hand-written line is a dead end in the editor, and the button says what each gap means. The extension composes text into a line rather than only replacing a value, so it must know where a flag goes in a hand-written line and can malform one whose shape it misjudges, and it moves furthest from the draft's rule that the extension composes no line.

On the recipe button, each line adds only the values its text carries, a shell step, the slot line, and a line of an unknown command adding nothing. In the line editor, every line of a known harness gets model and effort controls, a missing value shown as the harness default, and setting one inserts the flag into the line's text ahead of its closing `;` and any `# interactive` comment; every other line is shown as its text, read-only. The button stays as short as the values written allow and needs no mark vocabulary, while the editor lets the person write the missing flag, after which the button shows it. The button cannot tell a harness default from a step outside any harness, and the looped recipe's button shows its name alone; the editor still composes text into hand-written lines, with the misplacement risk that carries.

On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each other gap (`default` for a missing model or effort on a known harness, one fixed mark for a shell step or a line of an unknown command), while the slot line `<single-task line>` adds the harness, model, and effort read from the named single-task lines the looped run may choose for a task. In the line editor, only a line of a known harness carrying both flags gets model and effort controls; every other line, the slot line included, is shown as its text, read-only. The looped recipe's button shows the models and efforts its tasks can actually run on, the one recipe whose single line otherwise says nothing about them. Drawing the button needs the single-task lines, and for an exact set the rule file's assignments, read at every redraw, and the values shown are per task rather than per variant, so the label can name combinations a given run never uses; how single-task lines appear in the settings view is a sibling's choice this leans on.

alternative.id: Resolve slot line, editor adds flags

open-question.alternative: On the recipe button, each line adds the values it carries and a fixed mark for each other gap (`default` for a missing model or effort on a known harness, one fixed mark for a shell step or a line of an unknown command), while the slot line adds the harness, model, and effort read from the named single-task lines the looped run may choose. In the line editor, every line of a known harness gets model and effort controls, a missing value shown as the harness default, and setting one inserts the flag ahead of the line's closing `;` and any `# interactive` comment; every other line, the slot line included, is shown as its text, read-only. The fullest reading: every button says what each line runs on, the looped recipe included, and every known-harness line can have its model and effort set. It carries both costs at once: the button depends on reading the single-task lines and rule file at every redraw, and the editor composes flags into hand-written lines it may misplace, the largest departure from the draft's rule that the extension composes no line.

open-question.question: The settings view checks, enables or disables, and holds model and effort lists for each harness. The shipped recipe file holds lines for Claude Code (`claude`) and Antigravity (`agy`) only; a Codex line can stand only in a person's own recipes, and what a Codex line's plain print opens with, on which the runner's reading of a headless line depends, was never checked. Does the settings view cover Codex as a third harness, or Claude Code and Antigravity only?
open-question.alternative: The settings view covers Claude Code and Antigravity only: it runs no check for Codex, offers no enable or disable for it, and holds no Codex model or effort list. The extension reads no Codex line's harness, model, or effort. A `codex exec` line in a person's own recipes stays a line of a harness the extension does not know. Codex coverage is postponed, not ruled out: it waits on the unmade check of what a Codex line's plain print opens with, which stays recorded under `ideas/vscode_extension_follow_up.md` beside the deferred shipped Codex recipes. It matches what the extension ships and what the runner is known to read. Every line in `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` opens with `claude` or `agy`, so the view has no Codex-specific flag rules to write or test: Codex takes `-m` rather than `--model`, has no effort flag, and its permission flag is different too. Nothing in the view offers a harness whose headless lines might stop every chain they head. A person who runs Codex lines in their own recipes gets no harness check for Codex, even though `codex plugin list -m gurita --json` already returns the installed copy's version at once. Those lines get no model editing and no enable or disable either. How such lines appear on a button and in the line editor depends on how the unreadable-lines question is settled.

The settings view runs the harness check for Codex as it does for the other two: the CLI is found through the runner's shell, the installed Gurita copy is read from `codex plugin list -m gurita --json`, and that copy's version is compared with the packaged one. The result is shown as Codex's status. Codex gets no enable or disable and no model or effort list, and the extension reads no Codex line's harness, model, or effort, so a Codex line stays a line of a harness the extension does not know. The print check stays unmade and recorded in the follow-up file. It reports whether Codex's Gurita copy is installed and current, which is useful whatever the runner can read. It uses only the one fast, machine-readable query already confirmed on this machine. It does not depend on the unmade print check, because it neither offers nor rewrites a Codex line. The settings view would treat its three harnesses unevenly: one is checked but cannot be enabled, disabled, or edited. That departs from the goal's description of a view that does all of that for each harness. The view also shows a status for a harness whose lines the person still cannot manage there. How a failed Codex check acts depends on how the failed-check question is settled.

Codex is a third harness in the settings view, handled like the other two. It is checked through `codex plugin list -m gurita --json`, it can be enabled or disabled, and it holds a model list. Its lines are recognised by `codex exec`, and the line editor rewrites their model through `-m`. Codex holds no effort list, since Codex has no effort flag, so a Codex line carries and is offered no effort. The print check stays unmade and recorded in the follow-up file. The runner keeps reading Codex lines by its one rule for all hosts. Every harness the plugin ships a tree for is covered alike, and this fits the goal's per-harness wording. A person who already runs Codex lines in their own recipes can manage them in the same place and the same way as their Claude Code and Antigravity lines. The view would offer, enable, and edit lines whose headless print the runner has never been shown to read. If Codex's print opens with a banner or session header, every such line stops its chain as an unlisted line, and the runner stays as it is. It also adds Codex-specific parsing and rewriting (`-m`, no effort, a different permission flag) for a harness no shipped recipe uses. Where the Codex model list comes from depends on how the list-source question is settled.

Codex is a third harness in the settings view, with the same coverage as the full option above: the check through `codex plugin list -m gurita --json`, enable and disable, a model list rewritten through `-m`, and no effort list. On top of that, the mission makes the unmade print check: it runs a short headless `codex exec` line whose skill ends on a known fixed line and records what its plain print opens with. It also brings `ideas/vscode_extension_follow_up.md`'s entry up to date with that outcome. The runner stays as it is. The view offers Codex alongside the other two only once it is known whether the runner can read a Codex line's print, so the coverage rests on a checked fact rather than an assumption. The check also settles a question the follow-up file has carried since the first version. It adds to the mission a check that lies outside its goal. If the print does not open with the fixed line, the mission is left with a covered harness whose headless lines stop every chain, while the runner, which the goal keeps as it is, cannot be changed to read them. It carries the same Codex-specific parsing and rewriting cost as the full option without the check.

open-question.question: The settings view holds a model list and an effort list for each harness, and no file of the extension or the plugin lists them today: `claude` has no command that prints its models, while `agy models` prints one line per pair of model and effort. Where do the lists come from (values shipped with the extension, the values the recipe lines carry, a query of the harness, or the person's own entries), and can the person add and remove entries?
open-question.alternative: Source: the extension ships one model list and one effort list per harness as a constant in its own code or a bundled file (for `claude` the aliases `fable`, `opus`, `sonnet` and the efforts low, medium, high, xhigh, max that `claude --help` gives; for `agy` the base model ids and efforts `agy models` printed on 2026-11-22). Editing: none; the person cannot add or remove entries, and the lists change only with a new extension release. The simplest and most predictable form: no process is started to build a list, nothing extra is stored per user, the lists are identical on every machine and pinned by the extension's unit tests, and they work when a harness is absent or its query fails. The lists go stale as soon as a harness adds or retires a model (`agy models` already lists models no recipe uses), a full `claude` model name or a newly released model cannot be chosen without a release, and the extension now holds model names and effort levels, which the design draft recorded it would not (a revision the Design draft revision question owns).

Source: the extension ships one model list and one effort list per harness, as in the fixed form. Editing: the person can add entries and remove entries in the settings view; the additions and the removals are stored per user as an overlay on the shipped lists, so the list shown is the shipped list minus the person's removals plus the person's additions, and a shipped entry added by a later release appears unless the person removed it. Gives a working list on first open with no setup and no harness query, lets the person reach a model or full name the shipped list lacks or hide one never used, and still lets later releases' corrections reach every person. Two layers to merge and explain (a removed shipped entry must be remembered as a removal, and an added entry that a release later ships becomes a duplicate to fold), a per-user store for the overlay (where it lives is the Harness state store question's), and the shipped part still goes stale between releases and places model names in the extension.

Source: the extension ships one model list and one effort list per harness, used only to fill a person's lists the first time the settings view needs them. Editing: from then on the lists are the person's own stored copy, every entry added or removed freely, and no later shipped list changes it. One plain list per harness that the person fully owns, with no overlay rules: what the settings view shows is exactly what is stored, and the first open still offers sensible values. A later release's corrected or extended list never reaches a person whose copy already exists unless a reset is added, so lists drift apart across machines and versions, and the copy needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: no list is shipped or stored; each harness's model list and effort list is read afresh, on every re-read of the pane, from the `--model` and `--effort` values the lines of the shipped recipes, the person's own recipes, and the stored variants carry, grouped by each line's harness. Editing: none; an entry appears or disappears only as lines using it are added, edited, or deleted. Nothing new to maintain or store and nothing to go stale on its own: the lists are always exactly the values the person's runs already use, and the extension still writes down no model name or effort level of its own. Only values some line already carries can be chosen, so a model or effort no line uses (`gemini-4-neon`, `low`, `max`) is unreachable from the settings view and must first be written into an own recipe by hand, and deleting the last variant using a value removes it from the list; the values found depend on reading each line, which the Unreadable lines question governs.

Source: each harness's lists are read from the `--model` and `--effort` values the shipped recipes', own recipes', and stored variants' lines carry, as in the fixed form. Editing: the person can add entries no line yet uses and remove derived entries from the offer; the additions and removals are stored per user as an overlay on the derived lists. Keeps the extension free of shipped model names and keeps the lists tied to what is actually run, while letting the person reach a new model or effort without hand-editing a recipe file first. The first open offers only what the shipped lines use, so the person must type every other value themselves, a removed derived entry reappears in any new line that carries it unless the removal is kept as a standing hide rule, and the overlay needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: each harness's lists are the union of a list the extension ships per harness and the `--model` and `--effort` values the shipped recipes', own recipes', and stored variants' lines carry, so a value an own recipe uses (a full `claude` model name, say) is offered without being shipped. Editing: the person can add and remove entries, the additions and removals stored per user as an overlay on the merged lists. The widest offer with the least typing: the shipped part covers values no line uses yet, the derived part picks up whatever a person's own lines already run, and the overlay covers the rest. Three sources to merge, with the most rules to state, test, and explain (which removal hides which source, how a derived value that is also shipped is shown), the shipped part still goes stale between releases, and the overlay needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: Antigravity's lists are read from `agy models`, its `id<TAB>name` lines split into each base model id and the efforts it is printed at; Claude Code's lists, which no `claude` command prints, are shipped with the extension (the aliases and the efforts `claude --help` gives). Editing: none. Antigravity's list is exact and current on the person's own machine, including which efforts each model takes, so a line is never offered a model the installed harness lacks, with no list for it to maintain anywhere. Two mechanisms per harness; the query starts an `agy` process (when and through what shell are the Harness check timing and Harness check shell questions'), depends on an unversioned print format, and yields no list when `agy` is absent or fails; Claude Code's half still goes stale and cannot reach a full model name; whether the per-model efforts the query gives are kept per model is the Effort list granularity question's.

Each harness gets the most accurate source it has, and the overlay closes the gaps both leave: a full or newly released `claude` model name, or an `agy` entry to hide or to keep when the query is unavailable. The most moving parts of any option: a harness process per query with its own timing and shell (the Harness check timing and Harness check shell questions'), an unversioned print format, a shipped half that goes stale, an overlay over two kinds of source, and a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

open-question.alternative: Source: Antigravity's lists are read from `agy models`; Claude Code's are read from the `--model` and `--effort` values that the `claude` lines of the shipped recipes, own recipes, and stored variants carry, so the extension ships no model name or effort level for either harness. Editing: the person can add and remove entries on either harness, the additions and removals stored per user as an overlay. Keeps the design draft's rule that the extension holds no model name or effort level, while Antigravity's list stays exact from the harness itself and Claude Code's grows from what is run plus what the person enters. Claude Code offers only the values its lines already use (no `low` or `max`, no full model name) until the person types more, the `agy` query brings its process, timing, shell, and print-format dependencies (the Harness check timing and Harness check shell questions'), and the overlay needs a per-user store (the Harness state store question's).

Source: nothing is shipped, read from lines, or queried; each harness's model list and effort list starts empty and holds only what the person enters in the settings view. Editing: the person adds and removes every entry. The extension holds no model name or effort level and runs no query, so nothing it carries can go stale, and each list is exactly the person's deliberate choice with one store and no merge rules. open-question.question: On Antigravity the efforts a model takes differ by model: `gemini-4-argon` and `claude-opus-5-5` stop at `high`, while `gemini-4-neon` and `gemini-4-hydrogen` go up to `xhigh`, and a line naming an effort its model lacks stops when run. Is a harness's effort list one list for the whole harness, offered for every line, or kept per model, so that a line is offered only the efforts its model takes?
open-question.alternative: Each harness holds one effort list for the whole harness, and the line editor offers that whole list for every line of the harness whatever its model. The settings view holds no record of which model takes which effort, and a line given an effort its model lacks is accepted by the editor and stops when it is run, as a hand-written line does today. The simplest store and editor: one flat list per harness, matching the shape `claude --help` gives (one effort set, no per-model listing) and the lists the goal already names, with no per-model structure to keep, migrate, or fill in for models nobody uses. On Antigravity the editor offers `xhigh` and `max` for `gemini-4-argon` and `claude-opus-5-5`, which stop at `high`, so the settings view lets a person save a variant that is known to fail, and the failure shows only at run time, possibly part-way through an unattended chain.

Each harness keeps a list of models, each model carrying its own effort list, on both harnesses, and the line editor offers a line only the efforts its model takes. When a line's model is changed to one whose list lacks the line's current effort, or a stored or shipped line already names such an effort, the effort is kept as written and drawn marked as not taken by its model until the person picks one of the offered values. A line edited in the settings view cannot be given an effort its model lacks, matching the per-model pairs `agy models` prints (an effort-less id such as `gemini-pro-orchestrator-neon` carrying an empty list), while nothing the person wrote is changed without their action and a mismatch already present is visible rather than hidden. Every model needs its own effort list, which on Claude Code no command reports, so the per-model lists there are either copies of one set or entries someone must keep; how they are filled turns on the sibling list-source question, and the editor and store need a model-to-efforts structure and a marked state for a mismatched line.

alternative.id: Per model, effort reset on model change

open-question.alternative: Each harness keeps a list of models, each model carrying its own effort list, on both harnesses, and the line editor offers a line only the efforts its model takes. When a line's model is changed to one whose list lacks the line's current effort, the effort is replaced at once by the highest effort the new model takes that does not exceed the old one (the model's lowest when none is lower), so every line the editor saves names an effort its model takes; a stored or shipped line already naming such an effort is drawn marked until edited. A model change can never leave a line in a state that fails at run time: switching `gemini-4-neon` at `xhigh` to `gemini-4-argon` yields `high` in one step, with no second pick needed. The editor changes a value the person did not touch, so a quiet downgrade (an `xhigh` task line becoming `high`) can go unnoticed and run at less effort than intended; it carries the same per-model lists, and the same dependence on the sibling list-source question for Claude Code, as any per-model option.

Each harness holds one effort list for the whole harness, and any model of that harness may optionally carry its own narrower effort list; the line editor offers a line its model's own list when the model has one and the harness list otherwise. A line whose current effort its model's list lacks keeps it as written, drawn marked as not taken, until the person picks an offered value. Restrictions are recorded only where a model is known to differ (the Antigravity models that stop at `high`), so Claude Code and any model without known limits stay one flat list, while the known Antigravity failures are still kept out of the editor. Two levels of list and a fallback rule between them make the store and the editor more involved than either pure form, and a model with no subset of its own is offered the whole harness list even when it in fact takes less, so the protection is only as complete as the subsets someone has entered or read, which turns on the sibling list-source question.

The granularity is fixed per harness rather than chosen once: Antigravity keeps an effort list per model, in the pairs `agy models` prints, and the line editor offers an Antigravity line only its model's efforts, while Claude Code holds one effort list for the whole harness offered for every Claude Code line. An Antigravity line whose current effort its model lacks keeps it as written, drawn marked, until the person picks an offered value. Each harness's list takes the shape that harness itself reports, per model where `agy models` gives the pairs and one set where `claude --help` gives one, so the settings view never asks anyone to invent per-model effort lists Claude Code gives no source for. The two harnesses are stored and edited in different shapes, so the editor carries two code paths and a third harness (whether Codex is covered is a sibling question) must be assigned one; a Claude Code model that does not take every listed effort is still offered all of them.

open-question.question: Variants are to be stored as literal lines in a per-user file. Where are the settings view's other values kept, each harness's enabled or disabled state and its model and effort lists: in that same per-user file, in VS Code user settings, or in the extension's own stored state?
open-question.alternative: Each harness's enabled or disabled state and its model and effort lists are kept in the same per-user file that holds the variants, in a part of that file set aside for harness values, so the settings view reads and writes one file for everything it holds; nothing goes into VS Code settings or the extension's stored state. One store for the whole settings view: one file to read on every re-read of the pane, one write path, one place a person can open, back up, copy to another machine, or fix by hand, and a variant's model and effort sit beside the lists they are chosen from. The file must carry structured values that are not recipe lines, so its format has to hold a second kind of content and its reader must survive hand edits to it; how awkward that is depends on which file holds the variants and in what format (the Variant store file question), being worst if that is a person's hand-written Markdown recipe file. A machine-specific fact like whether a harness is enabled also travels wherever the file is copied.

All harness values are contributed configuration properties of the extension (for example one object per harness under a `gurita.` key), at application scope like the existing `gurita.ownRecipesFile`, and the settings view writes them to the user's global settings through the configuration API; the per-user file holds only variants. VS Code's own mechanism: a schema in the manifest validates the values, the person can read and edit them in `settings.json` or the Settings editor, the extension is told of changes made there, and Settings Sync carries the lists to every machine the person uses. The settings view's values are split across two stores, a file and settings, with no single place to see them together; object-valued settings show in the Settings editor only as an "Edit in settings.json" link; and syncing carries a harness's enabled state to machines where that harness is not installed, so its variants may show as enabled where they cannot run.

All harness values are contributed configuration properties written to the user's global settings, but each harness's enabled state is declared at machine scope, so it stays on the machine where it was set, while the model and effort lists are at application scope and sync; the per-user file holds only variants. Keeps every value in VS Code's validated, hand-editable settings while matching each to what it describes: whether a harness is enabled follows what is installed on this machine, and the lists, a person's preferences, follow the person. Two scopes to declare, explain, and test, on top of the split between settings and the variant file; a person setting up a second machine re-enables harnesses there; and the scope rules are VS Code behaviour the extension's tests, which run against a stub of the `vscode` module and never inside an editor, cannot exercise.

All harness values are kept in the extension's own global state (`globalState`, the store VS Code keeps per extension), written and read only by the extension, not synced across machines unless keys are registered for sync; the manifest contributes no new setting and the per-user file holds only variants. Nothing a person can break by hand and no schema or file format to define: the settings view is the one writer and reader, values are typed objects the code stores directly, and the stub-based tests can stand in for the store with a plain map. The values are invisible outside the settings view: a person cannot read, diff, back up, or copy them, they are lost with the extension's storage (an uninstall, a new profile), and the variants in a file can then name models the lost lists no longer hold. The extension today uses no stored state at all, so this adds a third kind of storage beside the recipe files and the one setting.

All harness values are kept in a second per-user file of the extension's own, separate from the variant file (for example beside it under `~/.gurita/`), in a format chosen for structured values, which the settings view writes and a person may edit by hand; nothing goes into VS Code settings or stored state. A plain, hand-editable, copyable file outside VS Code, as the variants are, without forcing structured harness values into the variant file's format, so each file keeps one kind of content and its own simple reader. A second file the extension writes and must read robustly against hand edits, with a second path to default and perhaps a second setting to move it, for what may be only a handful of values; whether that cost is worth paying depends on how many values there are to keep, which turns on whether the lists are person-editable (the Model and effort list source question). Its enabled state, like the variant file's contents, travels wherever the file is copied.

alternative.id: Enabled in state, lists in file

open-question.alternative: Each harness's enabled or disabled state is kept in the extension's global state, per machine and unsynced, while the model and effort lists are kept with the variants in the per-user file; the manifest contributes no new setting. Each value lives where its nature points: the enabled state, a fact about this machine's installed harnesses, stays on the machine and needs no format, while the lists, which the variants' lines are edited against, stay beside those variants in the one file a person can read and copy. Two stores for one view, one of them invisible, so a person reading the file sees the lists but not which harnesses are enabled; the variant file still has to carry a second kind of content, with the same dependence on that file's choice and format (the Variant store file question).

open-question.question: Every value a person types in the extension today goes through VS Code's input box, and nothing is typed on the pane's page. The settings view needs typed values, a variant's new name among them. Does it keep the input box for every typed value, or take text in fields on the page?

The pane today is a row of mission tabs ending in Refresh, New mission, and Define mission, with the selected mission's page beneath, and it holds no view that belongs to no mission. Where does the settings view stand in the pane and how is it opened: as a tab of its own in that row, behind a button that swaps the page for it, or as a part of every mission's page?

The settings view checks each harness by finding its CLI through a shell and reading its installed plugins from the harness's own `plugin list` command, so every check starts an interactive shell and a harness process. When does the check run: each time the settings view is opened, with every re-read of the pane, or only when the person asks for it?
open-question.alternative: The check of every harness runs afresh each time the person opens the settings view, its results drawn as they arrive and held only while the view stays shown; nothing is cached between openings, no separate check control is added, and reopening the view is the way to check again. No other re-read of the pane runs it. What the view shows is always as current as the moment it was opened, so a harness or plugin installed or upgraded from a terminal shows correctly the next time the view is opened, with no control to learn and no cached state to go stale. Every opening pays one interactive shell, whose startup files run each time, and one `plugin list` process per harness (66 entries for `claude` here, and a Codex listing that ran over a minute without `-m gurita`), so a person moving in and out of the view to edit variants waits on the same unchanged result again and again; and the result exists only while the view is open, which fails if the failed-check consequence (a sibling's question) has it act on the mission pages too.

The check runs as part of every full re-read of the pane (its opening, the Refresh control and command, a hidden stale panel shown again, a run's terminal closing, and a watcher burst that moves the live list), its results posted with each redraw; the watcher's in-process re-reads of one mission's documents do not run it, and the settings view shows the result of the latest full re-read. The results are always present wherever the pane draws, and they refresh after every run's terminal closes, so a Gurita copy installed or upgraded by a recipe run is picked up with no action of the person's, ready for any use the mission pages make of it. The heaviest cadence: a shell and harness processes start on every run's end and every Refresh, mostly to read a result that has not changed, and the check's latency or failure is tied to the re-read that draws the missions, so a slow harness listing can hold back or complicate every redraw of the pane.

alternative.id: Once per pane, lazily, with re-check

open-question.alternative: The check runs the first time the settings view is opened after the panel is created, and its result is cached for the panel's lifetime, shown on every later opening without running again; a check-again control in the settings view re-runs it on request, and no pane re-read or Refresh runs it. The cost is paid once per panel and only by a person who actually opens the settings view, while every later opening is instant and the person can still re-check after installing or upgrading a plugin. A result taken earlier in the session can be stale without sign (a plugin upgraded from a terminal reads old until the person presses the control or reopens the panel), and nothing is known about any harness until the settings view has been opened once, which fails if the failed-check consequence or the initial enabled state (both siblings' questions) needs the result on the mission pages.

alternative.id: Once per pane, eagerly, with re-check

open-question.alternative: The check runs once in the background when the panel is created, independently of the settings view and of the first mission read, its result cached for the panel's lifetime; the Refresh control and command and a check-again control in the settings view re-run it, while the watcher's re-reads, a hidden panel shown again, and a run's terminal closing do not. Across sessions the check costs almost nothing, since a harness setup changes rarely, while the settings view and the mission pages always have a result to show from the first moment. open-question.question: A harness's CLI is to be found through the runner's shell, the interactive session of the shell `$SHELL` names, whose startup files build the `PATH` a recipe line runs under.
